rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · A Wedding in the Greenwood
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a joyful woodland wedding beneath a vast ancient oak, garlands of oak leaves and wild roses, a young singer with a harp marrying a girl in a flower crown, a fat friar in brown joining their hands, outlaws feasting at long trestle tables, honeyed late-afternoon light through the leaves, storybook illustration

blocks.text: There came to the greenwood a young singer named Allan-a-Dale, with his harp on his back and his heart in trouble. He loved a lass of gentle birth, and she loved him too. But her father had promised her to an old knight with three times Allan's gold and none of his songs. And the wedding was set for the morrow.
A wedding under the great oak, with the whole greenwood for a congregation.
New word: officiate — to lead a wedding and make it lawful. The Bishop was asked to officiate, and made the best of it.

Robin held one rule higher than all the rest: no harm to any woman's happiness. "Dress me in your coat," he said to Allan, "and lend me your harp. Let us see what the church has to say about it." The next morning the famous Bishop of Hereford came riding to officiate. He found the church door pleasantly blocked by a herd of deer and a crowd of men in Lincoln green, who begged him, most courteously, to step inside and do his office quickly.

The Bishop did as he was asked, and did it well. Friar Tuck joined the hands, Allan sang, and the lass said yes with such a look that half the outlaws blew their noses. Then the whole company carried the couple into the forest. Under the great oak stood long tables, and venison, and honey cakes, and the best music ever heard between two trees.

They danced till the stars came out. "A wedding in the greenwood," said Robin, "is a fine way to mend a wrong thing. And we shall have need of all our mending soon, I think — for the Sheriff of Nottingham has not given up. And neither, my merry men, have we."

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Sheriff in the Greenwood
chapters.artPrompt: a proud sheriff in rich robes sitting stiffly at a long feast under a vast oak, outlaws in Lincoln green serving him venison on silver plates, a tall smiling archer raising a cup toward him, deer horns hung on the branches, green-gold evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: After the golden arrow was carried out of Nottingham at noonday, the Sheriff of Nottingham swore he would hunt Robin Hood down, whatever it cost. He raised a troop of men and rode into Sherwood with hounds and bows. He found nothing all day but trees, and laughter somewhere among the leaves.
The Sheriff dines on venison in the greenwood, a guest against his will.

One evening, tired and cross and hungry, the Sheriff met a quiet young forester leaning on a staff. "Give me a silver penny," said the young man, "and I will lead you to Robin Hood himself." The Sheriff's eyes gleamed. He paid the penny, and followed the forester deeper and deeper into the darkening wood.
New word: forester — a man whose work is in the woods, keeping the deer. This one kept them so well that even the Sheriff got lost.

Then the young man put a horn to his lips and blew a long, clear note. Out of the trees stepped a hundred men in Lincoln green, and the Sheriff's own soldiers were nowhere to be seen. "You are my prisoner," said the forester, taking off his cap, "and I am Robin Hood. But first you shall be my guest, for it is supper time."

So the Sheriff sat down under the great oak, and ate venison off silver plates. There was white bread, ale and red wine, and he swore between helpings that he had never dined better. When the feast was done, Robin took him kindly by the hand. "Go home, Sheriff," he said. "Keep the peace with my men, and no harm shall touch you." Then he had the Sheriff's horse led away — and his fine boots too, for a keepsake.

Next morning the Sheriff woke on a hillside far from anywhere, in his stockings, with a long walk before him. He walked home to Nottingham, and the boys in the street laughed all the way. From that day he hated Robin Hood twice as much — and feared him three times as much.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Guy of Gisbourne
chapters.artPrompt: two swordsmen clashing with great two-handed swords in a green forest clearing, one in Lincoln green and one in a strange shaggy coat of horsehide, sparks and flying leaves, tall trees leaning over the fight, fierce afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One morning the forest was full of a strange story. A hired swordsman called Guy of Gisbourne was riding through Sherwood in a coat of horsehide, with a two-handed sword. He was vowing to carry the Sheriff the head of Robin Hood. "Then he and I are hunting the same quarry," said Robin mildly. "So let us see which of us hunts the better."
Robin and the man in horsehide fight a long, ringing duel among the trees.

They met in a green clearing, and it was the hardest fight of Robin's life. The great swords rang like hammers, back and forth among the trees, till arms ached and breath failed. At last Guy's foot slipped on the moss, and Robin's blade struck home. The man in horsehide never rose again. Robin stood a while to get his wind back, for he had none to spare.

Then Robin did a bold thing. He took the coat of horsehide for a disguise, and walked into Nottingham in Guy's place, with Guy's sword at his side. The Sheriff greeted him like a hero, for he had work for him. Three of Robin's own men lay in chains in the market square, and the Sheriff meant to have their heads at noon.
New word: swordsman — a man who fights with a sword. Guy of Gisbourne was a famous swordsman, but even famous men can meet their match.

"Give me the work," said the man in horsehide, "I have a steady hand." So he was led to the square, with the axe at his belt and the crowd holding its breath. When he stood close beside the prisoners, he cut their ropes instead of their heads. And three clear notes of a horn rang out over the town.

Over the walls came the men of the greenwood, and through the gates with a storm of cheering. The Sheriff ran one way, the guards ran another, and three young men rode home free. As for the coat of horsehide, Robin hung it on the branch of an oak, where the crows could come and look at it.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Sir Richard of the Lea
chapters.artPrompt: an old grey-bearded knight kneeling with tears of gratitude before a table under a vast oak, a tall outlaw in Lincoln green counting out golden coins piece by piece, merry men watching kindly, venison and ale on the board, warm dappled light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One day Robin sat at dinner in the greenwood when an old knight came riding down the road. With him came only a poor little train of followers, and his face was full of care. Robin welcomed him as he welcomed everyone, and set the best of everything before him. For his rule was that no guest, rich or poor, should ever go unfed at his table.
Robin counts out four hundred golden pounds for Sir Richard under the great oak.

The knight was Sir Richard of the Lea. Trouble had brought him into a great debt, and four hundred pounds were owed to a proud abbot by tomorrow's sun. If the money was not paid, the abbot would take Sir Richard's castle and lands. Then the old knight would have nowhere left to lay his head. "I have nothing left," he said, "but my good name."

Robin counted out four hundred golden pounds on the table, piece by piece, and pushed them across. "Pay the abbot, Sir Richard," he said, "and bring me back my gold in a year and a day. If you are true to me, we shall be friends for life." The old knight took the money with tears in his eyes, and rode away like a new man.
Talk together: Robin lends his gold to a stranger and trusts him to bring it back. Ask your child: what made Sir Richard worth trusting?

Sir Richard rode to the abbey and laid the money before the abbot, counted piece by piece, on the very day it was due. The abbot's face fell, for he had been hoping to keep the lands for himself. And all that country laughed for a week at the proud abbot, who was outwitted by an honest man.

When a year and a day had gone past, Sir Richard came riding back to the greenwood with the gold in a bag. He brought gifts of wine and hawks for the band as well. "I would rather lose everything I have," he said, "than be unfaithful to Robin Hood." And the merriest feast of the whole year was held under the great oak that night.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The King in the Greenwood
chapters.artPrompt: a broad-shouldered traveller in an abbot's dark robes riding a palfrey on a forest road, a tall archer in Lincoln green stepping politely into the way with hand outstretched, merry men with drawn bows half-hidden among the trees, green morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last the news of Robin Hood came to the King's own ears. The Sheriff had lost his boots, his prisoners, his temper — and been sent home in his stockings. "If my men cannot take this outlaw," said the King, "I shall go and look at him myself." So he put on an abbot's robes, and rode into Sherwood with a few trusty knights dressed as monks.
The King, dressed as an abbot, is politely stopped on the greenwood road.

Sure enough, out of the trees came Robin Hood with a score of his men. "Stay, worthy abbot," said Robin, "and pay a small toll, for we take a piece of silver from every churchman who passes this way." The abbot counted it out gravely, as if it hurt him to part with it. And Robin, who was in the best of humours that day, invited the stranger to dinner.

It was the great greenwood feast again: venison and white bread, ale and red wine, and a hundred Merry Men waiting on the table. After the meal Robin called for his bow, and offered a golden coin to any man who could split the willow wand at fifty paces. One after another the finest archers in England split it clean. The quiet abbot watched with growing wonder in his eyes.
New word: toll — a small payment for passing along a road. The greenwood road had a toll of its own, and the abbot paid it.

"By my faith," said the abbot at last, "these are the finest archers I ever saw, and you must be their master. Show me your face, Robin Hood." Then the abbot threw back his hood, and there stood the King of England. Every man in the greenwood dropped to his knees at once, and Robin knelt lowest of all.

"Rise up, Robin," said the King, laughing like a boy let out of school. "I have come to pardon you and all your men — if you will serve me as faithfully as you have served one another." Robin promised it with a full heart. And that night the greatest guest in England slept under the great oak of Sherwood.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The King's Pardon
chapters.artPrompt: the greatest woodland feast at night under a vast oak, blazing fires and torches, a king in travelling robes laughing on a bench beside a tall archer in Lincoln green, outlaws dancing and drinking to a toast, bunting of green cloth between the trees, starry sky, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The King rode back to Nottingham with the merriest band ever seen at his heels. The Sheriff came out to meet them, white as milk, expecting to lose his post and his head together. But the King only laughed. "Here is the man you could not catch," he said. "And I have not caught him either. I have made a friend of him."
The greatest feast of all, with the King's health drunk at every table.

For a season Robin and his men served the King at court, and the court had never been so merry. But the men of the greenwood pined for the wind in the trees, the smell of the ferns, and the birds singing at dawn. Robin himself began, more and more, to look north and think of Sherwood.
New word: court — the king's own household, where lords and ladies gather. Even the merriest court cannot smell of ferns and morning rain.

The King understood, for a king who had dined under their oak could understand them well. "Go back to your greenwood, Robin," he said at last, "and shoot my deer no more, unless you ask me first." He gave Robin his hand, and Robin kissed it. And the two of them laughed together like a pair of schoolfellows.

So the band went home to Sherwood with the King's pardon in their pockets and the King's friendship in their hearts. Under the great oak they held the greatest feast of all: venison and honey cakes, music and dancing. The King's health was drunk in ale and red wine till the stars came out and the fires burned low.

And so the greenwood was free and glad again, as it had been from the very first day. The proud were never safe from laughter, and the poor were never turned from the door. A song went up from Sherwood that travellers carried to the ends of England — the song of Robin Hood, the merriest man that ever drew a bow.
